e.t: Abadia is a personal name, also rendered Avathia. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:9. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine what is said about the person there. Its normal function is therefore as a proper name preserved in the biblical record.

This Greek LXX noun means “brother,” naming a brother in relation to another person. It is a relational word used throughout the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus. With 786 occurrences, it is used broadly rather than being limited to one book or setting. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a brother. The surrounding verse determines the particular relationship being discussed, but the word itself identifies the person as a brother.

This adjective means “praiseworthy”: worthy to be admired, honored, or spoken of with approval. It describes a person, thing, or quality that deserves praise rather than blame. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times across ten verses, including passages concerning God’s greatness and human excellence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the person or thing it describes, but its central idea remains deserving commendation.

This Greek LXX adjective means “uncalled; unbidden.” It describes someone who has not been summoned or invited, emphasizing that the person has come or acted without receiving a call. As an adjective, it describes a person or situation rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Esther 4:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains the absence of an invitation or summons.

Alsōrēch, also rendered Alsorikh, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as an identifying name in the Greek LXX text and appears only once in that corpus, at Judges 16:4. Since a proper name identifies someone or something without stating its nature, the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what it names there.

This word means “capture”: the taking or securing of a person, place, or thing. It is a noun, so it names the result or reality of being captured rather than describing the action as a verb. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 27:46. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation and emphasis there.

This adjective means “carefree”: free from worry, anxiety, or troubling concern. It describes someone or something not weighed down by care. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, the word occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central sense remains a condition of being untroubled or unconcerned. It is a descriptive word, not a command or action, and identifies a state marked by freedom from care.

This Greek LXX verb means “brave deeds,” describing the performance of courageous actions. It presents bravery as something a person does, not merely a quality they possess. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense remains the carrying out of brave deeds.

This word means “thanksgiving,” referring to an expression of grateful praise. It is a noun, so it names the act or offering of giving thanks rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 17:27. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains the giving of thanks. This word therefore points to gratitude expressed toward God or in worship.

This Greek LXX verb means “interject” or “exchange.” It describes an action in which something is put into an exchange, especially within spoken interaction. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 11:13. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the precise force of the action in that passage must be determined from its sentence and immediate setting.

This adverb means “once,” referring to something that happens on a single occasion. It marks an action or event as occurring one time rather than repeatedly. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 40 times, showing a consistent temporal meaning across many passages. The word appears from Genesis through 3 Maccabees, including uses rendered “once” in Genesis 18:32, Leviticus 16:34, Numbers 17:10, and Judges 16:18 and 16:28. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words.

This noun means “captivity; exile,” referring to the condition of people removed from their homeland and living under displacement. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, all in seven verses, with occurrences in 2 Kings and Ezra. The word therefore describes exile as a settled condition or state, rather than simply the act of leaving. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “drip”: to fall or release liquid in small drops. It describes liquid gradually coming out rather than pouring all at once. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Joel and Amos, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. As a verb, it describes the action itself; the larger significance in either passage depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

This noun means a “seal” or “signet”—an object or mark used to identify, authenticate, or secure something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Jeremiah and once in Ezekiel. Its central idea remains the distinguishing mark associated with a person or possession, while the surrounding verse determines its particular use. The word is rendered “seal” in both recorded occurrences.

This word means “commander-in-chief,” referring to a person who holds supreme authority over an army or military forces. It is a noun naming a senior leader rather than an ordinary soldier or subordinate officer. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times across 16 verses, including passages connected with human military leadership and the heavenly army’s chief commander. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Asor is a proper name, identifying something called “Asor” rather than expressing a general quality or action. It appears fourteen times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with most occurrences in Joshua and additional occurrences in Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 1 Maccabees. The name is rendered “Asor” in the available English support. Its specific referent in any passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

e.h: A Personal Name: Aua or Ava
e.t: This word is a proper name, referring to a person or place called “Aua” or “Ava.” It is a name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 19:13. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the individual or location named there.

Baithanath, also rendered “Vethanath,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX text, it identifies a named entity in Judges 1:33. The gloss gives both “Baithanath” and “Vethanath” as the name’s renderings. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, so its ordinary function is simply to identify that name; its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Bari” or “Vari.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:36. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes its designation but does not provide further information about the person or the passage. Its precise significance there belongs to the verse’s wider context.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprout”: to begin growing or to spring up, especially as a plant or living growth emerges. It describes the visible beginning of growth rather than a completed mature state. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical books, including passages about plants, trees, and renewed growth. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the emergence of life and growth.

This noun means “herd,” referring to a group of livestock or other animals kept together. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used across 20 verses, especially in passages concerning herds as part of a household’s possessions, offerings, or prosperity. Its basic sense remains concrete and collective: not one animal, but a herd viewed as a group. The word appears from Exodus through Amos in the Old Testament Greek corpus.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Gai” or “Ye.” It names a person rather than describing an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 33:6. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide further details about the person or explain the surrounding verse. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the wider context of the verse and chapter.

Golela is a noun used as the name “Golela,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 2:13. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included, this lexical entry identifies the name but does not establish its precise referent there. That particular identification belongs to the context of the verse itself.

This Greek word means “discuss” or “lecture.” It describes speaking with others in a purposeful way, whether through conversation, instruction, or formal address. As a verb, it expresses the action of engaging people with words rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears six times, so its basic sense is clear while its exact force depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “divide”: to separate something into distinct portions, groups, or parts. It can describe an action in which something formerly together is distributed or set apart. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, appearing across books such as Genesis, Psalms, and 2 Samuel. Its precise force—whether dividing people, land, possessions, or something else—depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means to divide or separate— to put things apart rather than leave them joined together. It can describe the distinguishing or setting apart of things, people, or areas. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 24 times, including passages in Genesis concerning distinctions made in the created order and the separation of people or places. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided and the surrounding context.

Ebrona, also rendered Evrona, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 33:34 and Numbers 33:35. The name is preserved as a name instead of being translated into an ordinary English concept. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a named designation.

This adjective describes someone or something as “wearied”—worn down, tired, or lacking strength. It presents weariness as a condition rather than an action, helping identify the state of the person or thing described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Job, Ecclesiastes, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central meaning remains a state of weariness or exhaustion.

This noun means “inroad” or “entrance”: it refers to entering or to a way of access into a place. It can describe an actual doorway, passage, or approach, while “inroad” can emphasize movement into an area. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 43 times, so its basic sense is used across many settings rather than being limited to one passage. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the opening itself, the act of entering, or access through it.

“From there” is an adverb that points back to a place, direction, or location already understood in the sentence or surrounding passage. It tells where someone or something comes from or the point from which movement or action proceeds. This word occurs 134 times in the Greek Septuagint corpus, including passages from Genesis through later deuterocanonical writings. Its exact reference—what place “there” identifies—comes from the surrounding context of each verse.

This Greek LXX verb means to “clean out”—to remove what is present so that something is cleared. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in Deuteronomy and once in Judges. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the deliberate removal or clearing out of something.

This verb means to “dispatch out” or “send out.” It describes the act of sending a person or something away from one place or situation. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, it occurs eight times, including passages in Genesis, Samuel, Proverbs, and Baruch. Its basic sense is purposeful sending or releasing, while the surrounding passage determines who is sent and why. The word is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This verb means to have the flesh stripped off—that is, to describe flesh being removed from something. It is a physical action word, not a general term for harm or injury. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 24:4; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular force there. Its wording focuses on the removal of flesh, presenting the condition or result rather than naming the person who performs the action.

Elisous, also rendered Elisus, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 5:15. The available wording provides the name itself but does not establish an additional lexical meaning or explain the person’s role. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, not on a broader abstract definition of the name.

This LXX noun means “such and such,” referring to a person or thing that is left unnamed or identified only generally. It functions as a substitute designation rather than giving the person’s or thing’s specific name. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 6:8. Its basic sense is therefore brief and indefinite: it points to someone or something understood in the situation without naming it directly.

This verb means “look at” or “look in.” It describes directing one’s eyes toward something, or looking within something, depending on the sentence. It is a word of visual attention rather than merely being present or noticing something accidentally. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 20 times, showing regular use for focused looking across different passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the person is looking toward or into.

This noun means a “pledge” or “surety”—something given as a guarantee for an obligation or promise. It describes security connected with a debt or responsibility, rather than the debt itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Deuteronomy 24:10–13. Its precise force in any individual sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is a pledged guarantee or security.

gl: from in here; from this/that side
d: from in here; from this/that side

e.t: This Greek LXX adverb means “from in here” or “from this/that side.” It points to a place or direction from which someone or something comes, often marking movement away from a location or side. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains origin or direction: starting from here, or coming from a particular side. It occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees.

This Greek LXX adverb means “sudden,” describing something that happens abruptly or without warning. It modifies an action or event by showing that it occurs quickly and unexpectedly, rather than gradually or after a long delay. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in two passages from Proverbs and one from Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.h: To Disdain or Set at Naught
e.t: This verb means to disdain someone or something—to treat it as unworthy of regard or to set it at naught. It expresses rejection, contempt, or the refusal to value what is before you. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: regarding someone or something with contempt rather than honor or esteem.

This noun means an “enchanter” or “charmer”: a person associated with enchantment or the use of charms. It appears 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. The word serves as a label for such practitioners, rather than describing an ordinary skill or occupation. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb describes something dangerous or risky—something that may lead to harm, loss, or an uncertain outcome. It expresses the quality of being unsafe rather than naming a particular danger. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Wisdom 9:14. Its basic sense remains concise: what is dangerous or risky requires caution and cannot be treated as secure.

This noun means “wilderness,” referring to a wild, uninhabited, or desolate place. It names a setting rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, appearing in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Wisdom, Baruch, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a place marked by isolation, barrenness, or lack of settled habitation.

This adjective describes someone or something that is well-known or familiar. It points to what is recognized and known rather than unknown or obscure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Proverbs, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the surrounding verse determines exactly what person or thing is being described. The word appears in Proverbs 3:15, 5:6, and 33:26.

Ētham, also rendered Itham, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word with a translated meaning. It identifies a named figure or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek Psalms, at Psalm 73:15. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

Thara is a proper name used as a personal designation, not a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the name is rendered simply “Thara.” It occurs 11 times across 9 verses, chiefly in Genesis, with additional occurrences in Joshua and 1 Chronicles. The listed Genesis occurrences span Genesis 11:24–31, showing that the name belongs to the genealogical and family-history material found there. Its meaning is therefore its identity as the name Thara, rather than an abstract quality or ordinary vocabulary term.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a person’s will or desire—the intention, preference, or purpose someone has. It can describe what a person wants or chooses, and its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Daniel, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its central idea remains the inward desire or decision that directs a person’s action.

This adjective describes someone who is bold of heart—innerly confident, daring, or self-assured rather than timid. It points to a person’s inward disposition, especially the courage or boldness expressed through the heart. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Proverbs, so its ordinary meaning is focused and consistent rather than broad or varied. The surrounding verse determines whether this boldness is being commended or exposed as a fault.

This LXX word means a throne: the seat of a king or ruler. It is a noun for the place where a ruler sits and from which royal authority is expressed. The meaning is literal when it refers to a physical seat, and it can also point to the office or position of rule represented by that seat. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 153 times, making it a well-established term for royal rule.

Iasiph, also rendered Iasif, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies a person in Joshua 19:29. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, so its meaning is chiefly its role as an individual’s name, not a broader concept developed through repeated usage. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what is said about this person.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iezekiēl” or “Iezekil.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs five times: three times in Old Testament passages and twice in deuterocanonical books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Imalkoue, also rendered Imalkue, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or other named individual in the Greek LXX corpus. This name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:39. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or explanation of its name-origin. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This verb means to speak as an equal, addressing someone without placing oneself beneath that person. It describes equal standing expressed through speech rather than simply referring to equality as an abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning is speech offered on equal terms.

This Greek LXX noun means “bad experience.” It names an experience understood as adverse or difficult, rather than an action or person. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Malachi and three times in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains an experience involving hardship or trouble. The word is attested in Malachi, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees.

καταβοάω means to “cry down” or “cry out against” someone. As a verb, it describes forceful speech directed against another person, whether protesting against them or speaking them down. This LXX word appears five times across Exodus, Deuteronomy, and 2 Maccabees, so its use is limited but spans both law and later historical writing. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “number.” It is a verb used when people or things are counted or assigned a place within a number. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Genesis, Numbers, and 2 Chronicles. Its basic sense remains focused on numbering rather than describing a person, object, or feeling. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being numbered, but the word itself expresses the act of numbering.

gl: set in a place; place in position
d: set in a place; place in position

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “set in a place” or “place in position.” It describes putting something where it belongs or assigning it a particular position, with the focus on purposeful placement. The word occurs three times in this Greek LXX corpus, across 1 Chronicles, Esther, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being placed and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “invitation.” It is a noun for an appeal or summons extended to someone, describing the act of inviting rather than the person invited. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in the Septuagint, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central idea remains an invitation or call addressed to someone.

This adverb describes something done by force or in a severe manner. It adds intensity to an action, indicating that it is carried out forcefully rather than gently or mildly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel and once in Proverbs. The exact force of the word in either passage depends on the action and surrounding wording, but its central sense remains forceful or severe treatment.

This word means “cup”: a vessel used to hold or drink liquid. It is a noun, so it names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Exodus, Numbers, and Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains consistent as a cup or drinking vessel, while the precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “employment; service”: work or duty carried out for someone or in an assigned role. Its usual English rendering is “service,” fitting the idea of active service rather than merely an attitude or intention. It occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Exodus, Joshua, Chronicles, and Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the specific duty or setting meant by the word.

This word means “ransomer” or “redeemer”—one who secures a person or possession’s release. It is a noun describing the person who performs that rescuing or reclaiming work. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 10 times, especially in Leviticus, where redemption language is associated with recovering property or freedom, and also in Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains someone who redeems by paying or acting to bring release.

Maela is a personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:18. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the significance of the name in that passage. Its meaning here is therefore best stated simply: Maela, a personal name.

Mallōtai, rendered as Mallote, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or group by name. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:30. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name’s specific referent cannot be identified further, but its basic function is clear: it serves as a personal designation.

This verb means “chew,” describing the act of repeatedly working food with the mouth. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Leviticus 11:26 and once in Deuteronomy 14:8. Both occurrences belong to passages that distinguish animals according to their observable eating characteristics, so the word identifies a physical action rather than an inward attitude or figurative idea. Its ordinary sense is simply to chew or masticate food. The exact force in either verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “magnitude” or “greatness”—the quality of being large in size, extent, or degree. It can name the impressive scale or elevated character of something, whether physical or otherwise. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 17 times, so its basic sense is broader than one particular passage. The surrounding verse determines what is great or significant in each use.

This verb means “transpose; shift”: it describes moving something from its established place or position to another. It is an action word, presenting the act of changing location or arrangement rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages from Deuteronomy, Ezra, 2 Samuel, Isaiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun refers to internment or exile: the forced removal of people from their homeland or place of residence. It describes being taken away and settled elsewhere, rather than making a voluntary journey. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages associated with the displacement of God’s people and the downfall of nations. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on confinement, removal, or life away from home.

This noun means “mystery”: something hidden or not readily understood. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it refers to a matter whose meaning or knowledge is not openly available without disclosure. The word occurs 17 times in this LXX corpus, including repeated use in Daniel 2. Its basic sense remains focused on a mystery rather than on a specific kind of event, person, or object; the surrounding passage determines what particular mystery is being discussed.

Naasson is a personal name used for a specific biblical person, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 9 verses, from Exodus through 1 Chronicles, including several passages in Numbers. The English rendering preserves the name as “Naasson.” Its exact significance as a name is not defined by the lexical information here; the surrounding verse identifies the person being mentioned.

This verb means “wash”: to clean a person or thing with water. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly describes washing the body, hands, or feet, and it can also refer to washing connected with service before God. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 22 verses, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding context determines what is being washed and why. It is an ordinary action word, not a specialized term by itself.

Oziou is a proper name, also given as Oziu. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Chronicles, Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, and Zechariah. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise identity in each occurrence cannot be stated here, but its basic meaning is the personal name Oziou or Oziu.

This word means “house” or “household.” As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it can refer to a physical dwelling or to the people who belong to that household. Its 245 occurrences show that both uses are part of its normal range, with the surrounding passage determining which sense is intended. It appears throughout the Old Testament and also in the deuterocanonical books, including descriptions of homes, family units, and household settings.

This word means “soon,” describing something that will happen shortly or without a long delay. As an adverb, it modifies an action or event by indicating its timing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: three times in Old Testament books and twice in Wisdom. Its basic sense remains focused on nearness in time, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what action or event is expected soon.

“At dawn” means occurring in or belonging to the early part of the day, before the day is fully underway. It is an adjective, so it describes something connected with dawn rather than naming the time as a standalone noun. In the Greek Old Testament and Greek Wisdom text, it appears four times, showing a specific time-related use rather than a broad range of meanings. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This noun means “procreation of children”—the bringing forth or having of children. It names the act or process of producing offspring rather than a person who performs it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself has this focused meaning and does not describe children generally, parenting as a whole, or family relationships apart from the act of producing offspring.

This LXX Greek verb means to “keep watch” or “observe”—to look carefully and remain attentive. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both in Psalms, so its basic sense is focused and specific rather than broad. The surrounding wording determines how the act of watching or observing functions in each passage.

This adjective describes something held every five years, or quinquennial. It marks a recurring event or observance by the length of time between one occurrence and the next, rather than describing the event’s purpose or character. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:18. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular event being described there, but the word itself specifies its five-year interval.

This noun means “scum,” a term for something regarded as worthless, rejected, or fit to be cast aside. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 21:18. The word itself gives a strong negative description, portraying what is treated as refuse rather than something valued. Its precise force in Proverbs 21:18 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: scum or worthless refuse.

This word means “turning.” It is a noun describing a change in direction, movement, or position. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 50:5. The word’s basic sense is therefore an act or instance of turning rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains movement from one direction or position to another.

This noun means “rib,” the curved bone forming part of the side of the human body. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as an ordinary bodily noun rather than as a title, name, or action word. This LXX entity occurs twelve times across nine verses, including passages in Exodus, 1 Kings, Ezekiel, and Daniel. The word itself identifies the rib; the precise significance of a particular occurrence comes from its surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “how often”. It is an adverb used to ask about frequency—how many times something happens. In ordinary Bible reading, it points to repetition or the number of occasions rather than describing a person, object, or action itself. Within the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 62:2. The surrounding verse is needed to understand exactly how the question functions there, but the word’s basic sense remains a question about frequency or repeated occurrence.
